items.title: Doctoral Advising Guidelines by the AHM
items.summary:
[This is a guest post by the AHM communications group. — T.]

We are happy to announce that the Teaching Working Group of the Association for Human Mathematics wrote a set of recommendations on doctoral advising aimed at departments, advisors, and students. The document contains five guidelines centered on prioritizing human-authored writing, avoiding overreliance on AI, confronting the ethical concerns of AI use, and improving the wellbeing of students, as well as concrete proposals on how to implement them. We encourage everyone to read and share the document, and we especially look forward to feedback and suggestions.

Updates on my research and expository papers, discussion of open problems, and other maths-related topics. By Terence Tao

3 November, 2026 in guest blog , opinion | Tags: AI , Association for Human Mathematics | by Terence Tao

The proposal is very restrictive. Math with AI help can be a successful path, also for young scientists. Many here will not like to hear this: in chess, starting in the middle 1990’s, it took only about 10 years until ALL young people executed chess WITH computer help in their training sessions.

Back in 1986 Bielefeld University gave me a title “Dr. math”. Perhaps it is an idea to introduce a second doctoral title: “Dr. math-with-AI”.

items.title: EigenOrbit Study Compares 12 Quantum Computing Backends
items.summary:
Insider Brief

EigenOrbit’s research team has introduced eigenkit, an open-source Python library that lets developers run quantum algorithms across different simulators and hardware providers through a common interface.

The study evaluates 12 execution providers, including IBM Heron and IQM Emerald processors, and finds that no single backend performs best across all workloads.

The researchers found that simulator performance varies with circuit size and structure, while hardware performance also depends on how closely a circuit’s topology matches a processor’s physical connectivity.

PRESS RELEASE — A new study from the EigenOrbit research team examines a growing challenge in quantum computing: how to run and compare the same quantum algorithm across different simulators and hardware platforms without rebuilding the software workflow for each provider.

The paper,  “eigenkit: A Provider-Neutral Quantum Computing Library,”  introduces and evaluates eigenkit, an open-source Python library designed to separate the definition of a quantum algorithm from the backend used to execute it.

The study evaluates quantum workloads across  12 execution providers , spanning simulators and quantum hardware, and includes experiments on  IBM Heron  and  IQM Emerald  quantum processors.

items.title: FirstQFM Says Quantum System Beats Classical Forecasting Benchmarks
items.summary:
Insider Brief

FirstQFM reported that its quantum reservoir computing system, running on Rigetti hardware, outperformed the classical models evaluated in financial forecasts covering 43 anonymized assets and 600 out-of-sample periods.

The system achieved 52.02% directional accuracy and 112% higher cumulative gross portfolio profit than the strongest classical benchmark by profit, with an annualized Sharpe ratio of 1.22.

The evaluation used data anonymized by SW7 Group and chronological training, validation and test periods, with model selection based only on validation data.

Photo by Adam Śmigielski on Unsplash

PRESS RELEASE — FirstQFM today announced results from a financial forecasting evaluation in which its proprietary foundation-model-based quantum reservoir computing (QRC) system, running on Rigetti Computing ’s Cepheus -1-108Q system using data supplied by SW7 Group, outperformed state-of-the-art classical benchmarks across directional accuracy, macro-F1, gross portfolio P&L, and annualized Sharpe ratio.

The evaluation covered next-day forecasts across 43 anonymized assets and 600 out-of-sample periods. FirstQFM ’s foundation-model-based QRC system achieved 52.02% directional accuracy and 51.76% macro-F1, the highest results among the models evaluated.

items.title: Chicago Quantum Exchange Appoints Aaron Fluitt as CEO
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Aaron Fluitt has joined the Chicago Quantum Exchange (CQE) as its second CEO, succeeding Kate Timmerman, who led the consortium for eight years.

Fluitt previously held leadership roles at Argonne National Laboratory and PsiQuantum, where he worked on quantum research partnerships, manufacturing initiatives and workforce development.

He joins the CQE as it advances regional initiatives in quantum manufacturing, workforce development and research commercialization, including the $55 million Bloch Quantum Tech Hub.

PRESS RELEASE — Aaron Fluitt, a science and technology leader who helped drive Argonne National Laboratory’s successful effort to secure a $115 million award from the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to launch the Q-NEXT quantum research center, joined the Chicago Quantum Exchange today as the University of Chicago-based consortium’s second CEO. He succeeds Kate Timmerman, who oversaw the CQE’s growth from a nascent research collaborative to a 70+-member/partner organization that is building the world’s premier discovery-to-deployment quantum ecosystem.

A Quantum Prairie veteran known for his ability to rally diverse stakeholders, Fluitt brings a rich background that includes a PhD in molecular engineering from UChicago; leadership and strategy roles with PsiQuantum, Argonne, and the Boston Consulting Group; and a belief that strong partnerships accelerate innovation and growth for the emerging quantum economy.

“Aaron is a mobilizer, deep thinker, and recognized leader who has built relationships in nearly every corner of the quantum ecosystem. It is difficult to imagine someone more ideally suited to the mission of the CQE, particularly now, as we work to scale a manufacturing supply chain, lead unified quantum talent development, and, ultimately, pave the way for commercially useful quantum innovations,” said David Awschalom, the University of Chicago’s Liew Family Professor of Quantum Engineering and Physics, the founding director of the CQE, and a senior scientist at Argonne. “His experience across industry, national labs, and academia — combined with his impressive record of bringing bold ideas to life — will help catapult the CQE into its next phase of impact.”

items.title: Experiment Supports Theoretical Path to Topological Quantum Computing
items.summary:
Insider Brief

University of Cologne researchers observed quantum states consistent with theoretical predictions in a material system being investigated for topological quantum computing.

Measurements revealed highly transmissive Andreev states whose behavior across charge-carrier densities and under a magnetic field agreed with theory and simulations.

Confirming a transition to topological superconductivity requires more precise measurements of the predicted closing and reopening of an energy gap.

Electron microscopy image of the device under investigation. Pink: topological insulator; lavender: superconductor forming the Josephson junction, with a closed loop for magnetic phase control; gold: gold tunnel electrode used to detect the quantum states. (Jakob Schluck/Topological Matter Laboratory Cologne)

PRESS RELEASE — One approach to making information storage in quantum computing less prone to errors is known as topological quantum computing. It relies on special quantum states that are expected to be more resistant to local disturbances. Physicists at the University of Cologne have now observed quantum states that behave as predicted in a material system considered promising for this approach. Their findings, published under the title “Tunneling spectroscopy of topological insulator Josephson junctions” in Science Advances , support a theoretical description of how superconductivity interacts with the surface of a topological insulator.

Topological insulators are materials that insulate electricity in their interior but conduct it along their surfaces. When combined with a conventional superconductor, their surface states are predicted to support a special form of superconductivity known as topological superconductivity. If realized, this could provide a route to Majorana-zero modes, quantum states being investigated for their potential use in topological quantum bits, or qubits. Demonstrating and controlling these states experimentally remains a challenge.

items.title: Instanodes Develops Post-Quantum Account Solutions for Ethereum and Solana
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Instanodes has introduced post-quantum account implementations for Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)-compatible networks and Solana, alongside quantum-readiness assessments and custom cryptographic engineering services.

The implementations use hash-based digital signatures for account-level authorisation, with verification mechanisms adapted to the execution environments of each blockchain.

The company is targeting exchanges, custodians and blockchain protocols with services covering cryptographic assessments, migration planning and custom on-chain verification mechanisms.

PRESS RELEASE — Instanodes, a blockchain infrastructure provider offering RPC endpoints across more than 50 blockchain networks, dedicated nodes, validators and rollup infrastructure, today announced post-quantum account engineering for Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)-compatible networks and Solana. The expanded offering also includes quantum-readiness assessments and custom cryptographic engineering services for businesses evaluating their existing account security architectures.

Preparing Blockchain Accounts for Future Quantum Risks

Blockchain accounts predominantly rely on elliptic-curve cryptography for transaction authorisation. However, advances in quantum computing research have raised concerns about the long-term security of existing blockchain security architectures. Research published by Google Quantum AI in March 2026 and IonQ in September 2026 presented updated resource estimates examining how future fault-tolerant quantum computers could threaten widely used cryptographic methods.

items.title: When Not If: Coinbase Chief Sees Quantum, Not AI as The Biggest Threat to Crypto
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong said quantum computing poses a greater long-term threat to cryptocurrency security than AI and called for preparations against future attacks.

Coinbase is upgrading its custody infrastructure, while Armstrong urged blockchain networks to adopt quantum-resistant security.

Google researchers modeled a future quantum attack that could recover a private key in about nine minutes under specific assumptions, following advance preparation.

Image: Photo by PiggyBank on Unsplash

An argument is forming that artificial intelligence may be a bigger threat right now than the ominous introduction of future cryptographically relevant quantum computers.

Coinbase Global Inc. CEO Brian Armstrong weighed in during an earnings call and add his own two cents. He said quantum computing poses a more serious long-term threat to cryptocurrency security than artificial intelligence, as the company begins upgrading its systems to withstand future quantum attacks.

items.title: Universal Quantum Combines Ion Trap, Controls and Modular Links in New Chip
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Universal Quantum launched the iQPU, a trapped-ion quantum processor that integrates control technology and modular connections to support manufacturing and scaling.

The chip is fabricated on a commercial semiconductor foundry line and uses UQConnect interfaces to link processors into larger systems.

Universal Quantum plans to integrate the iQPU into customer systems, including two quantum computers under €67 million in contracts with the German Aerospace Center.

PRESS RELEASE — Universal Quantum launches the iQPU , an integrated quantum processing unit designed to make quantum computers practical to manufacture, scale and deploy cost effectively. Combining the largest trapped-ion compute surface with built-in ultra-low noise control technology and modular chip-to-chip interconnect (UQConnect) interfaces, the iQPU addresses some of quantum computing’s hardest scaling challenges and is a key puzzle piece of UQ’s route to utility scale quantum computing.

Quantum computing has advanced rapidly, but most systems were not designed to scale from the outset. As qubit numbers grow, each increase can demand substantial redesign across the architecture. Universal Quantum created the iQPU with a different philosophy: scaling is engineered into the system from the ground up.

“The question is no longer whether quantum computing can work, but how we build enough high-quality qubits to solve problems that matter,” said Sebastian Weidt, CEO and Co-Founder of Universal Quantum . “The iQPU allows us to combine our world record interconnect technology with a chip architecture that can control qubits at scale and is manufactured in commercial silicon foundries. It opens up an exciting route for us from today’s systems to the utility-scale quantum computers the world needs.”

items.title: SpecterAI and HPT Set Out PQC Migration Plans for Vietnam
items.summary:
Insider Brief

SpecterAI Quantum Security and HPT Vietnam Corporation have signed an implementation roadmap for their strategic partnership, covering post-quantum cryptography (PQC) migration services and quantum security training in Vietnam.

The partnership establishes three service areas: quantum security training, a five-phase PQC migration process, and compliance assessments against NIST and Vietnamese standards.

HPT will manage client relationships and migration implementation, while SpecterAI will provide technical support and independent validation, with initial training planned for HPT engineers before joint programs for banks and enterprises.

PRESS RELEASE — SpecterAI Quantum Security , a post-quantum cryptography (PQC) company, and HPT Vietnam Corporation signed the detailed schedules and action roadmap of their Strategic Partnership Agreement on October 28, 2026. The signing moves the partnership, first concluded in June 2026, from framework to execution, with a joint plan to bring PQC migration services and quantum security education to the Vietnamese market.

Post-quantum cryptography refers to encryption designed to withstand future quantum computers, which are expected to break public-key methods such as RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography. Organizations also face “harvest now, decrypt later,” in which encrypted data is collected today and decrypted later.

Under the agreement, HPT serves as a Preferred Partner of SpecterAI in Vietnam across three service pillars. The first is quantum security training, built on SpecterAI’s curriculum of 55 AI-proctored hands-on labs covering Shor’s algorithm, the ML-KEM and ML-DSA algorithms standardized as NIST FIPS 203 and 204, and VPN, TLS and PKI auditing. Training begins with HPT’s engineering team and extends to cohorts for banks and government agencies.

items.title: Germany’s Quint Raises 9.1 Million Euros to Develop Quantum Chips With Fewer Errors
items.summary:
Insider Brief

German quantum computing startup Quint raised 9.1 million euros in its first funding round to develop chips designed to reduce errors and lower error-correction costs.

Vsquared Ventures led the round, with participation from Quantonation , Nucleus Capital and industry specialists, including IQM co-founder Mikko Möttönen.

Quint plans to use contract manufacturers for production and must demonstrate that its chip architecture retains its advantages at the scale of hundreds of qubits.

Image: Quint Computing

German quantum computing startup Quint has raised 9.1 million euros in its first funding round to develop chips designed to reduce errors and lower the cost of building reliable quantum computers, Handelsblatt reported .

The financing, secured a little more than a year after the company’s founding, was led by Vsquared Ventures . Participants included Quantonation , Nucleus Capital and industry specialists such as IQM co-founder Mikko Möttönen, according to the newspaper.

items.title: Transformers Model Integration Contracts
items.summary:
On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture : a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study , the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

items.title: Egoless Mathematics in the AI Era
items.summary:
[This is a guest post by Karthik C. S. , Amit Sahai , and Jie Xue . This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

This is a good time for mathematicians to think carefully about the purpose of their work. The development of artificial intelligence brings that question before us with unusual force. Much of the discussion concerns which tasks machines will perform and which abilities will remain distinctively human. But our response also depends on a prior question: what do we understand mathematical work to be, and what gives it its worth? If our answer has become inseparable from the production of results and the demonstration of individual ability, the present uncertainty may reveal a difficulty in our conception of the work itself.

There are broadly two perspectives on mathematics. According to one, we invent it as we construct it: we introduce concepts, choose axioms, and develop theories. According to the other, mathematics exists independently of these activities, and our task is to discover it. These perspectives need not disagree about every aspect of mathematical practice. We plainly develop formalism and arguments. The deeper question is whether the truths we come to understand owe their existence to these acts, or whether our constructions enable us to recognize something that does not depend on us.

While discovery of mathematical truth can sound passive, a paleontologist searching for fossils must decide where to excavate, develop techniques, and recognize the significance of incomplete remains. The fossils existed long before the investigation, but finding them may require extraordinary imagination. Their prior existence gives direction to the investigator’s activity. Similarly, a mathematical discovery may require the invention of an entire language and framework through which a previously unnoticed relationship becomes intelligible. The discovery may require great creativity, but that does not make the truth discovered a creation of the individual. We encounter this distinction whenever our constructions surprise us. A definition introduced for one purpose reveals an unexpected connection elsewhere. A conjecture that seemed to organize our examples admits a counterexample. Two theories developed through different questions turn out to express a common structure. In each case, our thought encounters something it did not freely determine. We can revise our definitions or abandon our conjecture, but we cannot make the original argument valid merely by wishing it so.

The Platonic perspective gives a natural account of this independence. On this view, there were infinitely many primes before anyone proved that fact. Mathematical truth neither waits for our recognition nor receives its authority from it. We may choose how to describe a structure, but we do not choose its properties in the same way. This perspective also changes the place of the mathematician. Our intelligence becomes a means through which an order independent of us can be understood. The significance of the work lies in its relation to that order.

The distinction between a correct derivation and an understanding of its significance is equally important. An axiomatic system permits indefinitely many deductions, but the ability to produce them does not by itself supply a worthy direction of inquiry. Mathematical statements may be formally correct without being enlightening. We can introduce countless definitions and prove countless statements about them. What makes one definition illuminating? Why does one theorem disclose something fundamental while another merely adds to the available material? These questions concern the relation of a particular investigation to the principles it brings into view. Mathematical taste has a place here, provided we understand it as more than individual preference. We value a theory when it reveals a unity among things previously understood separately, or enables us to recognize why a phenomenon occurs. Although mathematical truths may exist independently of us, their discovery can transform our understanding and enrich our experience of the world. The ability to carry out longer chains of reasoning does not by itself explain such understanding. Reasoning serves understanding by articulating relationships and making their justification explicit. However, the success of reasoning does not mean that all knowledge can be reduced to it. Nor does our ability to reason more extensively determine what is worth knowing or why we seek knowledge.

Mathematics is only one field of knowledge. Not everything can be understood mathematically, nor is mathematical achievement the ultimate purpose of intellectual life. Yet we increasingly measure intellectual life through publications, citations, awards, and other indicators of performance. While useful, these measures become problematic when they define the worth of the work itself. We begin to see mathematicians…

items.title: Isogeny rigidity under algebraic group actions and finite translation orbits
items.summary:
We study finite orbits generated by fibrewise translations on varieties carrying two abelian fibrations.

Under natural dominance and generation hypotheses, non-isotriviality of the first family forces points with finite orbit to lie over proper closed subsets of both bases.

This extends results of Corvaja, Tsimerman and Zannier to complex families of arbitrary, possibly different relative dimensions, including torsors.

The proof combines relative Manin-Mumford with a general isogeny rigidity theorem for algebraic group actions.

items.title: Sonar-MoE: In-Backward Expert Updates for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Training
items.summary:
Most parameters of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model belong to its experts, and standard training keeps every expert gradient in GPU memory until the optimizer step. This memory grows with the number and size of the experts, so it rises as MoE models scale.

We introduce Sonar-MoE, which updates each expert tensor during the backward pass and frees its gradient right away. It brings optimizer-in-backward from dense models to batched MoE expert tensors, so the GPU never holds more than one layer of expert gradients.

When we fine-tune OLMoE-1B-7B and Granite-3.1-3B-A800M in bf16 with two expert-kernel backends, Sonar-MoE lowers peak memory by 19% to 22%. Its updates are bitwise identical to standard training without expert gradient clipping, and held-out loss stays within 0.003 of all baselines.

Each step also takes 17% to 23% less time than standard training with global-norm clipping. Updating whole batched tensors rather than individual experts is what keeps Sonar-MoE fast, as it avoids a 20% to 72% slowdown while using the same memory.

Sonar-MoE matches optimizer-in-backward over all parameters in memory and speed while still clipping the dense parameters.

items.title: Counterexamples to the Jacobian Conjecture from the viewpoint of lineability
items.summary:
Algebraic genericity in the family of polynomial counterexamples to the recently solved Jacobian Conjecture for $N\ge3$ is investigated.

The notion of affine-coneability is introduced and it is shown that this family is affine-coneable and 1-lineable, but not 2-lineable.

Semigroupability is further studied with respect to coordinatewise multiplication and composition.

items.title: Associated primes in group cohomology and a strange result
items.summary:
In 2010. Okuyama proved the following.

Let $G$ be a finite group and $k$ an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p$ dividing the order of $G$. (1) Let $\frak p$ be an associated prime of $H^*(G,k)$ of $\dim=s$.

Then there exists an elementary abelian $p$-subgroup $E\subseteq G$ of rank $s$ with $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak p_E$ and depth$\,H^*(C_GE,k)=s$. (2) Let $E$ be an elementary abelian $p$-subgroup of $G$ of rank $s$ and suppose depth$\,H^*(C_GE,k)=s$.

Then $\mathfrak p_E$ is an associated prime of $H^*(G,k)$. It is shown this result is true for all fields of characteristic $p$.

We also show the following result: If $E$ is an elementary abelian $p$-subgroup of $G$ and depth $H^*(G,k)=\text{rank} E$, then up to conjugation $E$ contains the maximal elementary abelian subgroup contained in the center of a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$.

items.title: GW/PT-correspondence for CY $4$-fold-II: Virtual Classes
items.summary:
Let $B$ be a complex manifold and $f:\bX\to B$ a derived \textit{complex-analytic} (not necessarily \textit{algebraic}) space with an oriented relative $(-2)$-shifted symplectic structure.

We suppose that the closed symplectic form is locally exact in the completed relative de Rham complex, and construct a derived smooth manifold over $B$, independent of additional choices. When $f$ is proper and oriented, this gives integral virtual fundamental classes on its fibres.

Our argument is heavily based on the strategy of Borisov-Joyce who already solved the \textit{algebraic} version of this problem, and uses \textit{derived differential geometry}. The proof also contains a relative analytic Darboux theorem a-la Brav-Bussi-Joyce, and has a natural analogue in Borel-Moore homology.

We provide applications to complex-analytic enumerative geometry: in particular, to counting Pandharipande-Thomas pairs on compact and non-compact complex-analytic Calabi-Yau $4$-folds.

This is part of a joint project with Felix Thimm dedicated to the proof of the GW/PT-correspondence for Calabi-Yau $4$-folds by implementing Pardon's programme in dimension $4$.

items.title: PlantVLM-Edge: Quantized Vision-Language Models for On-Device Crop Health Diagnosis
items.summary:
Timely and accurate crop health diagnosis is essential for sustainable agricultural production, yet accurate diagnosis often requires expert knowledge that is not readily available. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, and natural-language interaction, creating new opportunities for intelligent crop health assessment.

However, deploying VLMs on resource-constrained devices remains challenging due to their substantial computational and memory requirements. This paper presents PlantVLM-Edge, a quantized vision-language framework for conversational crop health diagnosis that can run entirely on resource-constrained edge devices.

PlantVLM-Edge combines agricultural domain adaptation, post-training quantization, and on-device serving with an offline chat interface, allowing growers to ask open-ended questions and receive diagnoses, symptom explanations, and management guidance without cloud connectivity. The framework is backbone-agnostic: we validate it with two different VLM types with varying scale and architecture (Qwen3-VL-2B and LLaVA-1.5-7B), four quantization schemes, and two diagnostic domains (plant diseases and insect pests), and we deploy all variants on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin.

Eight-bit quantization affects answer quality minimally relative to the full-precision model, and 4-bit activation-aware weight quantization (AWQ) retains 98.6% of full-precision answer quality on both domains while reducing the weight memory of the 2B backbone by 49%. In its most compact form, PlantVLM-Edge requires 2.01 GiB of weight memory, returns its first token in about 0.12 s, and completes a 64-token diagnostic response in 0.78 s.

These results demonstrate that timely and accurate crop health diagnosis is practical on edge devices, providing a foundation for next-generation crop monitoring and decision support systems.

items.title: Unifying entanglement and nonclassicality via the Narcowich-Wigner spectrum
items.summary:
Entanglement and nonclassicality are two fundamental features of quantum mechanics which serve as resources in quantum information processing tasks and are tightly connected by two-mode mixing.

In this work, we show that the connection between entanglement and nonclassicality extends well beyond the two-mode mixing setting by considering the case of arbitrary multimode Gaussian evolutions.

Using the Narcowich-Wigner spectrum as our main technical tool to quantify single-mode phase-space nonclassicality, we derive sufficient conditions for a single-mode state to generate NPT entanglement after a multimode Gaussian unitary evolution, which both tighten and generalize existing criteria.

As an application, we obtain simple single-mode protocols for quantitatively testing the entanglement structure of multimode quantum states over arbitrary bipartitions.

Our results identify the Narcowich-Wigner spectrum as a powerful tool for investigating fundamental properties of bosonic quantum states.

items.title: $C^1$-rigidity of $\mathbb{H}^{p,q}$-convex cocompact representations of Gromov hyperbolic groups
items.summary:
Let $p>3$ and let $Γ$ be a non-elementary Gromov hyperbolic group with $\partial_\inftyΓ\cong\mathbb S^{p-1}$. We prove that every $\mathbb{H}^{p,2}$-convex cocompact representation $$ ρ:Γ\longrightarrow \mathrm{PO}_{p,3} $$ whose proximal limit set $Λ_ρ\subset\partial_\infty\mathbb{H}^{p,2}$ is a $C^1$ submanifold preserves a totally geodesic copy of $\mathbb{H}^p\subset\mathbb{H}^{p,2}$.

Consequently, $Γ/\ker ρ$ is virtually a cocompact lattice in $\mathrm{Isom}(\mathbb{H}^p)$. For odd $p$, we prove the same conclusion for every signature $(p,q)$ with $p>q\ge2$, under the same hypothesis $\partial_\inftyΓ\cong\mathbb S^{p-1}$.

Our methods combine dynamics, differential topology, and representation theory. The key new ingredient is to study the radicals of the semidefinite forms induced on the tangent spaces of the limit set.

They form a continuous vector bundle of constant rank. The tangent action at attracting fixed points gives a bound, in terms of the radical rank, on the number of eigenvalues of an orthogonal lift whose modulus exceeds one.

We then use the topology of the sphere and the representation theory of real algebraic groups to exclude the remaining possibilities. In arbitrary signature with $p>q$, these arguments already imply that a representation with a $C^1$ limit set cannot be Zariski dense.

items.title: Library of Layers (LoL): Adaptively Ordering Transformer Layers at Runtime
items.summary:
Computer programmers chain together the same reusable computational primitives, for example, conditional statements or loops, but in different orders to implement different algorithms. In contrast, existing language model architectures always execute their layers in the same order.

We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), an architecture that dynamically orders its layers during inference to solve the problem at hand. LoL has a single hyperparameter, the size of its global library of transformer blocks, that allows it to transition seamlessly between parameter reuse and sparsity, generalizing the parameter-efficiency and FLOPs-efficiency tradeoffs of dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture of experts architectures in one unified family.

We show that LoL achieves competitive performance with all three above baselines when pretrained on text data. On synthetic sudoku and maze data, we observe that the model employs distinct layer orderings to implement different solution strategies, and we can intervene on routing to force a model to apply a specific solution strategy to a problem instance.

In a multilingual natural language setting, we find that LoL chooses different layer order patterns based on language and script. Similarly, we train LoL on safety data and fit probes to its router outputs, finding that these probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC.

LoL provides a path toward a future in which models dynamically compose their own computational graph, enabling more efficient and controllable reasoning.

items.title: Ask, Don't Equip: Question-Driven Coding Agents for Deep Kernel Optimization
items.summary:
LLM agents for GPU kernel optimization sit at two ends of a structure-freedom tradeoff. Scripted agents fix what the model does at each step, via a learned policy, an optimization menu, or fixed roles, and are sample-efficient where the recipe applies and stall where it does not.

Open-ended agents let a self-directed model mutate a population of kernels and pay for the freedom in trials: thousands of evaluations, repeated edits, and wrong candidates. Both respond to hard targets by equipping the agent with more: parsed profiler output, disassembly analysis, retrieval over documentation and libraries, and stores of lessons.

We argue that both lack direction, a hypothesis about where the remaining gap is, and that a short question asked at the right moment supplies it without narrowing what the agent may do next. We present KernelSeek, a question-driven agent that makes an existing CUDA kernel faster with no operator-specific knowledge and no faster implementation to imitate: a general-purpose coding agent, a minimal harness that enforces a verifiable goal, and questions at decision points, first from a human, then from a bank the agent applies to itself.

On the same task, evaluator, hardware, and week, a tool-rich autonomous agent built in the prevailing style plateaued at 0.50x FlashAttention-3 after 133 model-driven steps; KernelSeek reached 1.13x. It then produced dependency-free FlashAttention forward kernels for Hopper and Blackwell, single CUDA files with no CUTLASS, CuTe, cuBLAS, or cuDNN, correct on all 182 scenarios per architecture and 1.16x FlashAttention-3 and 1.46x FlashAttention-4 (geometric mean).

Across 162 human messages and 11.5K agent tool calls, every large gain followed a question that moved the agent to a different layer of the system or rejected a claimed limit, never one that supplied information. We release the kernels, harness, question bank, and all traces.

items.title: RASP: Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity Continual Learning in a Stationary-Size LoRA
items.summary:
Parameter-efficient continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers largely relies on a costly premise: preventing catastrophic forgetting requires either spawning a dedicated LoRA branch per session---causing adapter parameters to scale linearly with task horizon---or applying sparse Mixture-of-Experts gating symmetrically to both forward and backward passes, which sacrifices representational rank at test time. We argue that reading consolidated knowledge and writing new task credit are fundamentally asymmetric operations.

Because visual features in a shared low-rank space distribute across rank-1 atoms rather than localizing in disjoint task silos, forward inference should read all atoms at full rank capacity, whereas backward optimization should restrict plasticity to a sparse subset of input-aligned channels. We introduce RASP (Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity LoRA), which adapts a single stationary-size adapter across sequential tasks.

At each step, a scene-modulated cosine router selects the top-$q$ unlocked atoms to receive gradients, blocks updates on the remaining $r-q$ channels, and penalizes Frobenius Gram coherence between active and non-updated output directions. Across sessions, the router's empirical activation trace and each atom's exact spectral norm form a zero-overhead geometric consolidation index $ω_j = \sqrt{\tilde{c}_j \tildeσ_j}$ that drives Cauchy step attenuation and boundary anchor locking.

Across CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A, RASP matches or surpasses branch-expanding LoRA learners under a strictly constant parameter footprint.

items.title: Zeta functions of quasi-split reductive algebraic groups over local fields
items.summary: We calculate zeta functions of quasi-split reductive algebraic groups over local fields using the classification of Tits and prove a functional equation. We give explicit exam- ples of these zeta functions for non-split unitary and orthogonal groups.

items.title: Exceptional Points and Optimized Encoding in Qubit Stabilizer Codes
items.summary:
Continuous blind stabilizer measurements turn stabilizer codes into a Liouvillian spectral problem in which Hamiltonian terms compete with dissipative error channels. We show that this competition generically enables Liouvillian exceptional points, whose occurrence at weak error rates is constrained by the code distance.

Exceptional points are detrimental in this regime of error correction as they maximize the decay rate of encoded coherences. We then optimize the encoding of the logical qubit using the eigenmodes of the Lindblad operator.

This phase-optimized encoding cancels the linear short-time decay of logical qubit coherences. We apply this encoding to the [[5,1,3]] code and demonstrate that it outperforms naive encoding methods near the exceptional point, improves the fidelity of a logical $π$ rotation and remains effective in the presence of additional weak error channels.

items.title: Spectral pairs of Newton non-degenerate polynomials with isolated singularities
items.summary:
We give a formula for the spectral pairs of Newton non-degenerate polynomials with isolated singularities.

This is a revised version of a conjecture proposed by Steenbrink fifty years ago.

Although this conjecture fails in the non-simplicial Newton polytope case, we can find the correction term using the intersection complexes and the primitive intersection cohomologies of toric varieties associated with non-simplicial compact faces.

To verify the correctness of the formula, we provide a sample code for Singular which computes the spectral pairs and compares the output with that of sppairs in Singular for the three variable case.

items.title: Efficient thermalization of one-dimensional noncommuting Hamiltonians via system-bath interactions with $Θ(n)$ ancilla qubits
items.summary:
We prove rapid convergence of a system-bath interaction algorithm for preparing Gibbs states of one-dimensional noncommuting Hamiltonians at every fixed positive temperature. For a chain of $n$ qudits of local dimension $2^q$ with bounded nearest-neighbor interactions, the algorithm prepares the Gibbs state from any initial state to trace-norm error $0<\varepsilon\le1/2$ in expected total Hamiltonian evolution time $\widetilde{O}(n/\varepsilon)$.

This improves the previously proved $\widetilde{O}(n^6/\varepsilon)$ bound for single-ancilla system-bath Gibbs samplers, up to logarithmic factors. The proposed algorithm couples $4^q-1$ resettable bath qubits to each site in parallel and randomizes the interaction time.

Our analysis bounds both the one-round approximation error and the stationarity defect of an approximate stationary state in Gibbs-weighted $L^2$ norms, with only linear dependence on the system size. It also uses the dephasing induced by randomized evolution to control the extensive Lamb shift without treating it as a small perturbation of the dissipative dynamics.

items.title: NormMoX: A Normative Mixture of Experts for Explainable Autism Classification from Structural and Functional MRI
items.summary:
While structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI, fMRI) offer profound potential for researching autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and understanding individual neurodivergence, current classifiers lack the explanatory power needed for scientific study, clinical use and personal-level insights. Most models learn from imaging features that also vary with age, sex, scanner site and head motion. They fuse the two modalities without a common reference and explain decisions against arbitrary reference inputs rather than a typical brain.

We present NormMoX, a normative mixture of experts that makes the typical brain the shared reference for prediction, fusion and explanation. Normative models trained on large healthy cohorts give the value each brain measure is expected to take for a person's age and sex. NormMoX learns from each person's deviations from these expected values.

For each modality, a neural network expert turns the deviations into a score of evidence for ASD. A fusion head, MoX, compares each score with those of typical controls before combining them. It therefore needs no imputation when a modality is missing and shows in which modality each person is atypical.

On 1,035 participants of ABIDE I, NormMoX reached an AUROC of $0.728 \pm 0.004$ in repeated cross-validation, above linear, single-modality and deep fusion baselines. NormMoX thus shows not only whether a person is likely to have ASD, but where, and in which modality, their brain departs from typical. The implementation is available at https://github.com/Novelex/NormMox.

items.title: FLAMIA: FLAsh MIcroscaling Attention for Fast and Causally Safe Training on Blackwell
items.summary:
Attention remains a substantial computational cost in Transformer training, particularly at long context lengths. NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs provide high-throughput low-precision matrix multiplication, but exploiting it in attention requires addressing quantization overhead, causal information leakage through shared scales, and numerical inconsistencies between the forward and backward passes.

We present FLAMIA, a family of attention kernels for Blackwell with MXFP8 and mixed NVFP4/FP8 training paths. Our design combines token-block scaling that reuses quantized operands across matrix orientations, targeted safeguards against scale-induced leakage, and consistent forward and backward computations.

Fused quantization and architecture-specific kernel optimizations reduce overhead, while document-local scaling and workload-aware scheduling support variable-length documents directly in packed layouts without repacking. Across various causal packed-document workloads, the MXFP8 path accelerates the combined forward and backward attention call, including quantization, by factors of $1.10$--$1.40\times$ on B200 and $1.06$--$1.42\times$ on B300 relative to the fastest evaluated baseline for each workload.

We validate training stability and quality preservation on pretraining Llama-style models. These results show how jointly designing quantization, training numerics, and document scheduling translates low-bit hardware throughput into practical attention acceleration.

items.title: Geometrization of Kottwitz-Shelstad transfer and Vogan's conjecture on local Arthur packets
items.summary:
We give a geometric analogue of Kottwitz-Shelstad transfer for a general class of reductive groups over p-adic fields with cyclic component groups of trivial or prime order.

We prove that this geometric transfer coincides with Kottwitz-Shelstad transfer, adapted to the language of disconnected groups, assuming the local Langlands correspondence satisfying certain desiderata, including the Kazhdan-Lusztig hypothesis for the ambient group and its endoscopic groups.

As an application of this geometrization, we prove Vogan's conjecture on local Arthur packets over p-adic fields: for quasisplit classical groups and their pure inner forms, all local Arthur packets are ABV-packets, and the distributions attached to these ABV-packets of Arthur type satisfy Arthur's local conjectures on twisted endoscopic character relations.

This demonstrates the following general principle: for any reductive group G over a local field, an Arthur packet should be defined as an ABV-packet of Arthur type, equipped with the endoscopic pairing calculated by traces of actions on vanishing cycles or microlocalizations.

items.title: The SIMPLE Law for Energy Cost of LLM Inference
items.summary:
Generative AI is billed per token, yet tokens are not equally expensive. Each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so energy grows non-linearly along a sequence whose tokens look identical.

No analytical model states what a token costs, and the most accurate SOTA model is a fit, not a law: it absorbs architecture into fitted coefficients, requiring per-LLM fitting. We derive closed-form expressions of the computational and memory-access complexity of LLM inference in terms of architectural hyperparameters, covering MHA and GQA, and compare a family of analytical models of increasing granularity.

From these, we obtain the SIMPLE Inference Model to Predict LLMs Energy (SIMPLE), a four-parameter law that separates prefill from decode, and decode into KV-cache cost and next-token computation. Over traces of 13 dense LLMs from six families on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it attains R2 = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE, 3.1-3.5x below the SOTA, without per-LLM calibration.

The SIMPLE law explains as well as predicts: prefill energy grows quadratically with the hidden dimension, so larger LLMs suffer most from long inputs; and more aggressive GQA KV grouping reduces the per-token energy by up to 3x relative to standard MHA. Increasing the reasoning token budget pushes output length beyond the analytically derived energy minimum, driving super-linear energy growth; although accuracy grows with the budget, energy grows faster, so Intelligence per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14x across a 4.0x reasoning-budget range.

Agentic serving raises energy per request by 13.0x relative to non-agentic ones, driven by the growth of both the prefill and the KV-cache terms with input length; while prefix caching removes most of the prefill cost (-93%), the KV-cache term is unaffected, so even a cached agentic request costs 4.8x more.

items.title: Agentic Pipelines for Mapping Topological Codes to Quantum Hardware
items.summary:
Mapping a prescribed many-body Hamiltonian to a particular quantum hardware is generally an approximate process, resulting in both intended and unwanted quantum dynamics. We introduce an AI-agent-assisted workflow that uses Lean to establish whether an effective device Hamiltonian retains the intended low-energy subspace of the target many-body Hamiltonian. We demonstrate this approach with topological quantum error correction (QEC), providing, to our knowledge, the first Lean-verified pipeline connecting a code space to low-energy states of a device model.

Starting from qubits and parity checks, the pipeline constructs the ideal Hamiltonian whose lowest energy states form the intended code space, and determines the excitation gap that protects that code space. It then tests if the device retains the required number of isolated low-energy states and quantifies how closely their subspace matches the intended code space. We compare three bounds on unwanted energy shifts obtained by: summing the interaction strengths, grouping the anticommuting Pauli interactions, and diagonalizing the Hamiltonian.

Pauli grouping yields a bound that is tighter than the conventional sum and closer to the diagonalization result, avoiding overly conservative compensation requirements. The workflow also identifies the strongest unwanted interactions and the qubits they affect, providing specific targets for improving device couplings and controls. We demonstrate our framework using an eight-qubit toric-code array on a superconducting device, where the same driven device generates both the required four-qubit interactions as well as unwanted dynamics.

An AI agent identifies viable device parameters within a prescribed leakage budget, and Lean verifies four isolated low-energy states close to the ideal code space. Our workflow supports predictive hardware engineering for analog implementations of QEC codes.

items.title: Stabilizer Learning under Global Depolarizing Noise with Polynomial Copies and $2^t$ Time
items.summary:
We study learning the stabilizer structure of an unknown pure $n$-qubit state observed through global depolarizing noise of unknown strength, with a fixed promised upper bound below one, using destructive two-copy Bell measurements. Let $0\le t\le n$ bound the stabilizer nullity, let $\varepsilon>0$ be the accuracy, and let $0<δ<1$ be the failure tolerance.

With probability at least $1-δ$, a learner must return a commuting unsigned Pauli group containing every stabilizer of the pure state; averaging conjugation by that group must decrease the purity of the observed noisy state by at most $\varepsilon$. Tang and Steckmann gave such a learner with polynomially many copies and $2^t$ times polynomial time when the noise strength is below a threshold of at most about $0.16$, which tends to zero as $t/n\to1$.

They asked whether other algorithms with these resources can exceed this threshold. We answer this question affirmatively for every fixed bound on global depolarizing noise below one and every $0\le t\le n$, including states with only one promised independent stabilizer.

Our learner uses polynomially many copies and $2^t$ times polynomial classical running time. All resource bounds hold on every execution.

Their polynomial factors depend on $n,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/δ)$, with degrees and constants depending on the fixed noise promise.

items.title: FAU Researchers Test Quantum Machine Learning for Lung Cancer Prediction
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Florida Atlantic University researchers evaluated quantum machine learning methods for lung cancer prediction using a limited dataset of symptoms and risk factors.

A D-Wave quantum annealing-based support vector machine achieved the highest reported accuracy, reaching 94.31% in simulation and 91.90% on quantum hardware.

The researchers describe the findings as preliminary, noting that the dataset was augmented with synthetic samples and that further testing on independent clinical datasets is needed to assess generalizability.

PRESS RELEASE — Developing reliable machine learning models for healthcare can be challenging when only small datasets are available. This challenge motivates research into whether quantum computing approaches can learn useful patterns from limited symptom and risk-factor data.

A research team, led by Arslan Munir , Ph.D., professor in Florida Atlantic University ’s Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science within the College of Engineering and Computer Science , and director of the Intelligent Systems, Computer Architecture, Analytics, and Security Laboratory , evaluated quantum machine learning approaches in simulation and on quantum hardware using symptom and risk-factor data for lung cancer prediction under limited training data.

The study, published in Discover Quantum Science , a Springer Nature journal, “Inferring lung cancer under limited learning data through gate-based and annealing-based quantum techniques,” provides a common framework for evaluating different quantum machine learning methods under the same data preparation and testing conditions.

items.title: The Universal Nilpotent Cone and a Canonical 1-form
items.summary:
We construct a canonical Du Bois 1-form on the nilpotent cone in the dual Lie algebra of any reductive group.

Using this 1-form we give an intrinsic construction of Nadler and Yun's universal global nilpotent cone.

In particular, we obtain a moduli interpretation of the universal nilpotent cone.

items.title: A complete description of the algebraic structure of pseudocompact abelian groups
items.summary:
We solve a major open problem from [D. Dikranjan, D.

Shakhmatov, Algebraic structure of pseudocompact groups, Memoirs AMS 633 (1998)] by describing abelian groups which admit a pseudocompact Hausdorff group topology. First, we prove that an abelian group G can be equipped with a pseudocompact Hausdorff group topology iff it can be decomposed into a direct sum G=B\oplus H of a bounded torsion group B and agroup H satisfying |nH|=|H| for all positive integers $n$, such that both B and H admit a pseudocompact Hausdorff group topology.

Second, for an unbounded abelian group G, we denote by m the minimal positive integer n such that |nG|=|kG| for all integers k\ge n. Then G admits a pseudocompact group topology iff both G[m]={g\in G: mg=0} and mG\cong G/G[m] admit a pseudocompact Hausdorff group topology.

items.title: Qyantram: A Transparent and Verifiable Quantum Computing Platform
items.summary:
Most quantum circuit platforms focus on idealized circuit assembly and simulation, hiding hardware compilation, error identification, and variational model training behind black-box operations. QYANTRAM addresses this gap through an open platform comprising four subsystems, built around evidence-backed results and independent verification.

Its staged compilation pipeline makes every transformation traceable, while the router publishes rejected SWAP candidates and their scores for transparent decision-making. Verification exploits inactive qubits remaining in the |0> state, reducing complexity from 2^N to 2^k for k active qubits.

This mathematically exact reduction enables full pre-compilation verification on 127- and 156-qubit layouts, achieving approximately 10,000x speed-ups with execution times below one millisecond. The error identification engine exhaustively evaluates all Pauli error patterns without sampling, matching closed-form predictions within 2.8e-17.

Its machine-learning engine achieves numerical agreement within 2.0e-15 of qiskit.quantum_info while training 25-50 times faster. The router introduces approximately 1.27x more SWAP gates than Qiskit's SABRE due to its omission of optimization, trading routing efficiency for complete decision transparency and traceability.

items.title: Spin SYK-dot chains: entanglement bound and resource estimates towards a quantum advantage
items.summary:
Ground states of Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK)-type models are volume-law entangled, which makes them costly both for tensor networks and for quantum hardware simulations. Thus, it remains unclear where quantum hardware could outperform classical simulation of such models. In this work, we study a spin SYK-dot chain, in which q dense SYK dots of p qubits are joined by single ZZ bonds of strength K.

The entanglement across any cut is then bounded by floor(p/2) ln 2 plus the inter-dot entanglement, and the two-qubit depth of one Trotter step is set by p alone. A resource estimate shows that a quantum advantage for the ground state could appear only for dots of about 15 to 21 qubits or more. There, a single Trotter step already requires two-qubit error rates of order 10^{-6}, beyond the reach of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware.

We test the assumptions of this estimate with an imaginary-time matrix product state (MPS) that applies each dot as one block. It agrees with exact diagonalisation at (p, q) = (6, 2). At (5, 2), a variational circuit with the same dot-plus-link layout comes within 3.6% of the exact energy, and noisy simulations show that its fidelity decays as assumed in the resource estimate.

At (8, 5), i.e., N = 40 qubits, the energy converges at bond dimension chi = 768, far below the exact value 2^20, and the inter-dot entanglement stays small and is set mainly by K. Out-of-time-order correlators across the links decay on a time scale that shrinks rapidly with |K|. Thus, the dot size p and the inter-dot coupling K together set the entanglement of the chain, and with it where a quantum advantage could appear.

items.title: Hammock coordinates for silting subcategories of derived-discrete algebras
items.summary:
We introduce hammock coordinates to study the combinatorial structure of partial silting configurations in the bounded derived category of a derived-discrete algebra $Λ(r,n,m)$. By extracting exact integer inequalities from the Bobiński--Geiß--Skowroński Hom-hammock formula, we establish a closed-form criterion for pairwise partial silting both within any $\mathcal Z$-component and across distinct components.

Using this coordinate framework, we establish three primary results. First, we prove the universal upper bound $|S| \le n+m$ on the cardinality of any partial silting configuration $S$ of $\mathcal Z$-objects ---both globally via Bongartz completion in the silting-discrete setting, and combinatorially within a single component via a $Σ^r$-invariant staircase argument.

Second, we prove that this bound is universally sharp by constructing an explicit L-shaped partial silting configuration of size $n+m$ for every $Λ(r,n,m)$, alongside specialized diagonal configurations. Third, we show that the configuration lattice carries a faithful action of the cyclic group $\mathbb Z/g$ where $g = \gcd(r+m, n-r)$.

We conclude by showing a structural obstruction to local determination: pairwise partial silting of consecutive objects in the lattice ordering does not imply global partial silting, due to the strict additivity of a coordinate defect along chains.

items.title: How Many Qubits Would it Take to Simulate a Holographic Universe?
items.summary:
Insider brief

In the latest episode of The Quantum Kid, theoretical physicist Juan Maldacena of the Institute for Advanced Study explains the holographic principle. This is the idea that everything inside a region of space, gravity included, can be described by information on its boundary.

Maldacena estimates how many qubits a quantum computer would need to simulate a holographic universe. The qubits would have to be stable and near-perfect, closer to error-corrected logical qubits than today’s noisy physical ones.

The episode also visits Microsoft’s quantum lab in Copenhagen. There, Dr Lauri Sainiemi discusses Majoranas and Microsoft’s topological qubit approach to building more stable qubits.

Maldacena’s 1997 paper, which first set out the holographic duality, remains the most cited paper in the history of high-energy physics.

Quantum computing roadmaps usually talk about drug discovery, materials and optimisation. One of the most influential theoretical physicists alive has a different application in mind: simulating a universe.

In the latest episode of The Quantum Kid , Prof. Juan Maldacena of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton explains the holographic principle. This is the idea that everything happening inside a region of space, gravity included, can be fully described by information on its boundary. His 1997 paper turned that idea into a concrete mathematical model and remains the most cited paper in the history of high-energy physics.

items.title: Final coalgebras over R-modules
items.summary:
Final coalgebras and the coinduction principle for coalgebras over $R$-modules, where $R$ is a commutative ring, are essential in determining the denotational behaviour of various types of linear weighted automata. The goal of this paper is to provide lower and upper bounds on the ordinals that are needed to construct final coalgebras over $R$-modules as the limit of a transfinite sequence of functor iterations.

We give an example of a binary intersection preserving finitary functor on the category of abelian groups, which is the category of modules over integers, that fails to converge in $ω\cdot 2$ steps, thus settling an open problem of Adámek, Milius, and Moss. Then we relate this to the failure of the Artinian property of the integers and show that all finitary functors on $R$-modules for a Noetherian ring $R$ with Krull dimension $n$, which preserve countable directed intersections and a generalised notion of monomorphism, converge in $ω\cdot (n + 2)$ steps.

We also establish how the connection between Aczel-Mendler bisimulation and behavioural equivalence is mediated by the functor $\operatorname{Ext}^1$. These results show that homological algebra tools can play an important role in coalgebra.

items.title: Correlated Catalysis Removes the Strong Converse for Entanglement Distillation
items.summary:
Entanglement distillation converts noisy shared quantum states into maximally entangled pairs using local operations and classical communication. The distillable entanglement $E_D$ determines the maximum asymptotic rate at which this process can be performed reliably.

For several classes of quantum states, distillation above this rate obeys a strong converse: the fidelity with the target state vanishes asymptotically. Here we show that correlated catalysis removes the strong converse for every distillable bipartite state.

Specifically, at any target rate $R>E_D$, the optimal asymptotic fidelity is given by $E_D/R$. Thus, although catalysis does not increase the maximum reliable distillation rate, it allows nonvanishing fidelity at every finite rate.

Remarkably, this advantage persists even when the catalyst is returned exactly at every finite blocklength and the correlations between the output and catalyst vanish asymptotically. We further characterize the catalyst size required to sustain nonvanishing fidelity above the reliable distillation rate.

items.title: HKUST and HKMA Launch PQC Toolkit for Banks
items.summary:
Insider Brief

The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) have launched a Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) Toolkit to help banks plan their transition to quantum-safe cryptography.

The toolkit provides guidance and practical tools for assessing cryptographic assets and dependencies, setting migration priorities, assigning responsibilities and developing transition timelines.

The initiative supports the HKMA’s goal of raising the banking sector’s Quantum Preparedness Index (QPI) from 2.3 out of 10 in July 2026 to 10 by 2030.

PRESS RELEASE — The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) and The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) today (2 November) launched the Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) Toolkit (Toolkit), with support from industry participants. The Toolkit sets out a structured and comprehensive framework to guide banks in planning and advancing their PQC transition journeys.

The Toolkit supports banks in establishing clear governance and accountability, assessing cryptographic exposure, identifying transition needs, as well as monitoring implementation progress.  The Toolkit also brings together key planning considerations to facilitate an orderly and risk-based transition.

In particular, the Toolkit includes a suite of practical tools to help banks get started with practical assessment and planning, such as taking stock of their cryptographic assets and dependencies, defining transition priorities, strengthening engagements with suppliers and developing practical transition timelines accordingly.

items.title: DepthGraft: Structural Regularization through Hierarchical Cross-Layer KV Reconstruction
items.summary:
Scaling depth is a key route to stronger large language models, but Pre-LN architectures often suffer from depth-wise information dilution, limiting the effective use of deep layers. While cross-layer connectivity has proven effective at mitigating this problem, existing designs usually introduce additional computation or memory access. We revisit cross-layer KV sharing as an efficient form of such connectivity.

Beyond cache compression, each KV reuse edge creates a direct gradient path from deep layers to source KV projections, turning KV sharing into an implicit structural regularizer for KV representation geometry. We provide a systematic analysis of this mechanism, showing that proper sharing topologies sharpen key retrieval directions while enriching the value content subspace, whereas existing adjacent or global-anchor designs do not fully exploit this effect. Motivated by this, we propose DepthGraft, a hierarchical KV-sharing architecture that reconstructs deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallow-middle source pairs.

DepthGraft distributes non-local gradient flow across source layers, while preserving prefill early completion and reducing KV cache by roughly one third. Experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters show consistent downstream improvements under both GQA and MLA. Notably, on the 16B MoE model, DepthGraft achieves a 7.0% absolute improvement on MMLU-Pro, along with gains of 6.6% on CMMLU and 6.4% on C3.

These results validate the potential of DepthGraft as a scalable design for large-scale pretraining. The project page is available at https://github.com/jianke0604/DepthGraft.

items.title: Belief Propagation-Informed Tesseract Decoding of Quantum LDPC Codes
items.summary:
In quantum error correction, the decoder must estimate the errors from the measurement data accurately and fast enough to avoid a backlog. Search-based decoders such as Tesseract achieve high accuracy by finding a minimum-weight set of error events with an A* search, but their search effort grows rapidly with the physical error rate and the code size.

To reduce this search effort while maintaining a logical error rate close to that of Tesseract, we propose a belief propagation (BP)-guided modification of the Tesseract decoder for quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Damped sum-product BP is applied to the triggered detectors before the Tesseract search.

If the detectors triggered by the BP hard decision match the triggered detectors, this hard decision is accepted directly, and the Tesseract search is skipped. Otherwise, the BP marginal probability estimates, weighted by a trust coefficient, modify the search priority, while the path cost keeps the channel-prior weights so that the decoding objective is unchanged.

The framework also supports BP-based initialization, in which selected BP decisions form the starting point of a residual search whose signed-cost objective allows incorrect initial decisions to be removed. A node-exploration limit bounds this residual search; if the limit is reached, the decoder falls back to the BP-guided search on the original triggered detector set.

The method is evaluated on the [[72,12,6]], [[90,8,10]], and [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle codes under circuit-level noise. With BP-based initialization and a global trust coefficient, the number of Tesseract search nodes expanded is reduced by up to more than two orders of magnitude at low physical error rates, while the logical error rate remains close to that of Tesseract.

items.title: Hodge--Riemann relations for $m$-positive and generalized $m$-positive forms
items.summary:
We study Hodge--Riemann relations for ordinary, sequential, and weak $m$-positive real $(1,1)$-forms in complex dimension $d$. For ordinary $m$-positive forms, we prove the fully mixed relations in every permitted bidegree without assuming semipositivity, generalizing results by Xiao.

As a generalization of ordinary $m$-positivity, sequential $m$-positivity is defined by the hyperbolicity cones of successive directional derivatives of the determinant. We formulate a generalized mixed Hodge--Riemann conjecture for this condition and prove several cases beyond the scalar inequalities supplied by hyperbolicity.

We also consider weak $m$-positivity which corresponds to the pointwise subsolution condition for the complex $m$-Hessian equation. In this setting, we prove the Hodge--Riemann relations for $p\neq q$ and in several diagonal cases, and show that the associated power map induces a pointwise diffeomorphism onto the cone of positive $(d-1,d-1)$-forms.

Using Dinh and Nguyên's $L^2$ globalization method, we pass from the pointwise relations to cohomology classes on compact Kähler manifolds. Finally, we propose conjectures on a numerical criterion for sequential positivity and on solvability of the generalized $m$-Hessian equation.

items.title: South Korea Launches Hangang Supercomputer, Plans Quantum Integration
items.summary:
Insider Brief

South Korea has brought Hangang, its sixth national supercomputer, into full operation, with the government expecting it to rank among the world’s top 10 systems.

Hangang has 8,496 GPUs and 9,936 CPUs, delivering 24 times the theoretical computing performance of its predecessor, Nurion, alongside improvements in storage and network capacity.

The government plans to connect Hangang with a quantum computer in the first half of 2027 to develop a hybrid computing system combining high-performance computing and quantum processing.

South Korea’s sixth national supercomputer, Hangang, is now fully operational, Seoul Economic Daily reported . The government expects the system to place among the world’s top 10 machines.

It also intends to pair Hangang with a quantum computer in the first half of next year, forming a hybrid system meant to speed up both calculation and optimization.

The Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) and the Korea Institute of Science and Technology Information (KISTI) said they held a launch ceremony on the 2nd at KISTI headquarters in Daejeon. Hangang succeeds Nurion, the fifth national supercomputer, which was introduced in 2018. The agencies said the ceremony opened a new phase for national infrastructure supporting AI-based science and technology research.

items.title: Diagonal Equivalence in State Space Models: Characterization, Retrieval Rank, and Selective Extensions
items.summary:
We classify real and complex state-space models (SSMs) with linear transitions, distinguishing fixed-basis diagonal equivalence from input-output equivalence and tracking coefficient-conditioning windows under coordinate changes. We characterize diagonal equivalence through commuting transition families whose members are diagonalizable over the chosen field. With time-shared token-local matrix maps, we identify this class's state-mediated kernels with unnormalized scalar-mode linear attention with multiplicative masks.

Mamba 3's multiple-input, multiple-output (MIMO) construction lifts one value per local interface; SSD-MIMO routes independent values for local retrieval rank above one. HybridMamba combines Mamba 1's per-coordinate decay, Mamba 2-style heads and Mamba 3's complex rotations and two-endpoint writes, mixing real and rotating state blocks with different decay laws. They recover Mamba 1-3 single-input, single-output (SISO) configurations as exact special cases.

On five large H100 bfloat16 workloads, our fused GPU kernels improve geometric-mean training time over official Mamba 1/3 in matched SISO recoveries, with Mamba 2 near parity at SSM-core scope. Memory tradeoffs depend on the baseline and metric: saved-for-backward versus peak allocation. In small-model multi-token recall experiments, both designs outperform Mamba 1-3 on the hardest tier; higher routing ranks perform best in gated or phase-diverse configurations.

In single-seed language models with about 500M parameters, both improve on Mamba 1/2 in test loss at 2B tokens, but the routing gains do not translate into lower language-model loss. Our best configurations approach Mamba 3 SISO through 10B tokens while remaining behind it and Mamba 3 MIMO in language-model loss.

items.title: Scottish Widows Targets Quantum Computing With UK Venture Growth Investments
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Scottish Widows is directing workplace pension savings into U.K. technology businesses, with Oxford Quantum Circuits and Quantum Motion among its expected initial investments.

Aberdeen Investments appointed IP Group to oversee the venture growth portfolio, which also expects to invest in battery company Nyobolt and healthcare business Genomics Limited.

Scottish Widows says the mandate aims to improve retirement outcomes and provide follow-on funding for British companies preparing to commercialize technology and expand.

Image: Photo by Andrew Dawes on Unsplash

Scottish Widows is directing workplace pension savings into British technology businesses, with two quantum computing companies among its expected initial investments.

The pension provider has announced its first investments in U.K. venture growth companies through a portfolio overseen by IP Group , Corporate Adviser reported. The initial investments are expected to include Oxford Quantum Circuits and Quantum Motion , alongside battery technology company Nyobolt and artificial intelligence-enabled healthcare business Genomics Limited.

items.title: Digital Finite Group Theory
items.summary:
This book develops a digital formulation of finite group theory, in which every finite group of order $N$ is represented as the alphabet $\{0,1,\dots,N-1\}$ endowed with the transported group product. Multiplication, inversion and related structure are written explicitly as integer operations on labels.

The foundations treat digit functions, codes of permutations and $r$-ary operators, finite magmas, and constructions of laws from diagrams. Classical parts of finite group theory, including conjugacy classes, stabiliser chains and characters, are recast as identities between digits of codes.

The book gives explicit digital laws for all groups of order at most 32, the finite quotients of the 17 plane and 230 space crystallographic groups, the symmetric and alternating groups, the finite simple groups of Lie type, and all 26 sporadic groups. For most sporadic groups the laws are obtained by chain constructions; for the Baby Monster and the Monster they are computed structurally from the 196884-dimensional representation and evaluated with the mmgroup package.

The accompanying software archive reproduces the laws, tables and worked examples as verifiable integer data.

items.title: VideoEditor-MoE: Scaling Complex Video Editing with Mixture of Experts
items.summary:
Complex video editing requires understanding complex instructions while jointly fulfilling multiple editing requests. Meeting these demands through dense model scaling substantially increases computational cost.

We introduce VideoEditor-MoE, the first open-source mixture-of-experts framework for video editing. Beyond sparse MLP-MoE layers, MoE-Attention expands attention capacity through routed key--value experts while preserving global interactions among video tokens.

Initialized from a 5B video editing model, VideoEditor-MoE scales to 14B and 56B parameters, with approximately 8B parameters activated per token in both variants. Comparisons with existing methods and two complementary baselines, Explicit-MoE and MLP-MoE, assess its benefits over explicit expert guidance and MLP-only expert architectures.

Further analyses demonstrate that all experts remain active and reveal that learned routing responds more strongly to sample content and diffusion noise levels than to human-defined editing categories. Spatial analysis further indicates sensitivity to object-level semantic features.

We also identify decoupled weight decay as a strategy for stabilizing expert scaling.

items.title: Nobel Laureate John Martinis to Deliver Quantum Computing Lecture at UWA
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Nobel Laureate Professor John Martinis will deliver a free public lecture at the University of Western Australia (UWA) on the development of quantum computing and the experiments behind superconducting qubits.

Martinis, who shared the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics with John Clarke and Michel Devoret, will discuss his early research and experiments that advanced superconducting quantum computing.

The November 10 lecture will cover how semiconductor manufacturing techniques and systems engineering could support the development of scalable quantum computers.

PRESS RELEASE — How quantum computing has evolved during the past 40 years from an intellectual curiosity to a potentially realisable technology will be the subject of a free public talk at The University of Western Australia next month by US Nobel Laureate Professor John Martinis.

Professor Martinis, from the University of California, was one of three scientists, including John Clarke and Michel Devoret to win the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics for “the discovery of macroscopic quantum mechanical tunnelling and energy quantisation in an electric circuit”.

He will describe his thesis work that led to the Nobel Prize, as well as several other important experiments that have advanced superconducting qubits, the basic unit of information in quantum computing.

items.title: Quantcore Welcomes Innovation Minister to Showcase Manufacturing Ambitions
items.summary:
